place.zh: 黑松岭 · 第二十七道记号
place.en: Black Pine Ridge · the twenty-seventh mark

_weather: 「暴雨里」 as it opens, then 「雨小了些」 — rain all through, easing; rain over storm for the longer part

setup.zh: 第二十七道记号那里，是一段贴着山崖的窄坡。爹的左膝盖罢了工，整个人往崖外一歪——离你两步，坡外是崖。
setup.en: At the twenty-seventh mark the path is a narrow slope hugging the cliff. Father's left knee gives way and he pitches toward the edge — two steps from you, and the cliff beyond.

recap.zh: 暴雨里，你在风歇的空当把爹拽回了山壁，自己却给甩下了崖，摔进谷底的厚苔藓：先查伤，再找路，活到爹来的时候。
recap.en: In the storm you hauled Father back against the rock in the lulls of the wind, and were flung over the edge yourself, into thick moss on the valley floor: check the hurts first, then find a way, and stay alive till Father comes.

zh: 贴着山崖的窄坡，第二十七道记号。
en: A narrow slope on the cliff; the twenty-seventh mark.
The wind comes in gusts, and lulls.

story.zh: 第二十七道记号那里，是一段贴着山崖的窄坡。他爹的左膝盖在这里软了一下，整个人便往崖外一歪。
story.en: At the twenty-seventh mark the path became a narrow slope hugging a cliff. Here his father's left knee gave way, and his whole body tipped towards the drop.

label.en: Haul Father back to the rock

exits.means: hauls father back against the rock face in a lull of the wind, is flung over the edge into the valley, checks his hurts, finds a fire-steel and a light

story.zh:
小满想都没想——不对，他想了，而且想得飞快：离他爹两步，坡外是崖；去拉他，爷儿俩可能一起下去；不拉他，他一定下去。这笔账，不难算。

小满扑将过去，一把抓住他爹的腰带，拼了命往里一拽；他自己却被那股劲一带，甩了出去。他爹回身伸手来抓，手指擦过了他的手腕，终究没抓住。

小满滚了下去。最后一下，他摔进了一片软乎乎的东西里，却是一层苔藓，极厚极软。{景=zhuigu}

他没有喊，只在心里算：爹被自己拽进了山壁里，没掉下来；他会等雨停了，顺着记号回村叫人。四十一道记号，是自己刻的，一道都没歪——除了第一道。所以要做的，便是活到那个时候。

他爹说过，打猎的人在山里迷了路，头一件事是找个地方躲雨，第二件事是生火，第三件事才是害怕。小满决定，第三件事先欠着。

他从地下摸起一片尖石头，扶着崖壁往前走。崖根底下的苔藓里，那片尖石头「当」地碰着了一样硬东西。他扒开苔藓，是一把火镰。火镰的木把上拿刀刻着一个字，他认得，是他娘教他写的头一个字：**沈**。石坳村姓沈的，只有一户；沈家进了黑松岭没回来的，只有一个。

爷爷到过这里——爷爷是在这道谷里没的。他把火镰和火石揣进了怀里。这件事，他跟谁也没说。

这山谷很是古怪。这里的树他却一棵也不认得，叶子银白，薄得透光。便在这时，他看见了光。山谷最深处，一片给雨水砸出来的浅坑里，有一点银光一明一暗，一明一暗，像有什么东西在很慢很慢地呼吸。
story.en:
Xiaoman didn't even think — no, that's wrong. He thought, and he thought fast: Pa two steps away, the drop past the slope. Pull him, and maybe they'd both go over. Don't pull him, and he'd certainly go over. It wasn't a hard sum.

Xiaoman threw himself forward, grabbed his father's belt and hauled inward with everything he had, and the force of it swung Xiaoman himself out and away. His father spun round and grabbed for him. His fingers brushed Xiaoman's wrist, and in the end they didn't catch it.

Xiaoman fell. At the last he landed in something soft. It was moss, a layer of it, very thick and very soft.{景=zhuigu}

He didn't shout. He just did the sum in his head: Pa had been hauled into the cliff face by him and hadn't fallen. He'd wait for the rain to stop, follow the marks back to the village, and fetch help. Forty-one marks, cut by his own hand, not one of them crooked — except the first. So what he had to do was stay alive until then.

His father had said that when a hunter gets lost in the mountains, the first thing is to find somewhere out of the rain, the second is to make a fire, and only the third is to be afraid. Xiaoman decided the third thing could stay owing for now.

He felt about on the ground for a sharp stone and went on along the foot of the cliff. In the moss at the foot of the cliff, the sharp stone struck something hard with a *clink*. He scraped the moss away. It was a fire steel. On the wooden handle of the fire steel a character had been cut with a knife, and he knew it. It was the first character his mother had taught him to write: **Shen**. In Shi'ao Village there was only one household named Shen, and of the Shens only one had gone into Black Pine Ridge and not come back.

Grandpa had been here. Grandpa had died in this valley. He tucked the fire steel and the flint inside his jacket. He didn't tell anyone about it, ever.

This valley was very strange. Here he didn't know a single tree. Their leaves were silver-white, so thin the light came through them. And then he saw the light. In the deepest part of the valley, in a shallow hollow the rain had battered out of the ground, a point of silver light was glowing and dimming, glowing and dimming, as if something were breathing very, very slowly.

story_full.zh:
小满想都没想——不对，他想了，而且想得飞快，快得像他娘拨算盘珠子：离他爹两步，坡外是崖；去拉他，爷儿俩可能一起下去；不拉他，他一定下去。这笔账，不难算。

说时迟那时快，小满扑将过去，一把抓住他爹的腰带，拼了命往里一拽，拽得他爹整个人撞在山壁上，「哎哟」一声；他自己却被那股劲一带，甩了出去。他爹回身伸手来抓，手指擦过了他的手腕，终究没抓住。

小满滚了下去。泥浆、石头、断枝、雨水劈头盖脸而来，天和地在他眼前翻了不知多少个跟头，翻得他连哪边是天都分不清了。他护住了头，后背撞上一样硬东西，疼得眼前一黑，伸手乱抓，竟抓住了一根藤。

那藤绷得笔直，硬生生把他往下掉的势头拽住了一下，跟着便断了。{景=zhuigu}

最后一下，他摔进了一片软乎乎的东西里，却是一层苔藓，极厚极软，像一床吸饱了水的大棉被。他整个人陷进去半尺深，好似一只掉进了大馒头里的蚂蚁。

他没有马上起来。他爹说过，摔了先别急着爬起来，一样一样地查。他先动动手指，手指能动；再动动脚趾，脚趾也能动；膝盖破了，手掌磨掉了一层皮，后背火辣辣的，左手腕肿得老高，断没断，他摸不出来，好在还能动。

他这才坐起身来往上看，崖壁高得望不到顶，一直隐进了雨雾里。

他没有喊，只在心里算：爹被自己拽进了山壁里，没掉下来；他膝盖不好，这么大的雨，他下不来，也不该下来；他会等雨停了，顺着记号回村叫人。四十一道记号，是自己刻的，一道都没歪——除了第一道。所以要做的，便是活到那个时候。

十二岁，一个人，在一个从没来过的山谷里，天又快黑了。他爹说过，打猎的人在山里迷了路，头一件事是找个地方躲雨，第二件事是生火，第三件事才是害怕。小满决定，第三件事先欠着。

雨小了些。他从地下摸起一片尖石头，扶着崖壁往前走，每走一段，便在崖壁上划一道，好记得回来的路。

走出去不到半里，崖根底下的苔藓里，那片尖石头「当」地碰着了一样硬东西。他扒开苔藓，是一把火镰，锈得通红，鞘子早烂没了，旁边一块火石拿油布裹着，油布也烂了一半。

火镰的木把上拿刀刻着一个字，刻得歪歪扭扭，他认得，是他娘教他写的头一个字：**沈**。他蹲在那里，看了很久。石坳村姓沈的，只有一户；沈家进了黑松岭没回来的，只有一个。

他想起吴婆婆那句「你爷爷走的那年，也从我这门口过」，手心一阵发凉。爷爷到过这里——爷爷是在这道谷里没的。他把火镰和火石揣进了怀里。这件事，他跟谁也没说。

这山谷很是古怪。外面的山长的都是松树、柏树、野栗子，这里的树他却一棵也不认得，叶子银白，薄得透光，雨水落上去也不往下淌，滚成一颗一颗圆溜溜的珠子挂在叶尖上。

他没忍住，伸手碰了一颗，只听得「叮」的一声轻响，像一只极小极小的铃铛，那珠子化作一缕白气，散得无影无踪。

地上的草也不一样，每一步踩下去，草叶都微微发亮，一圈淡淡的光从他脚底下漾开，又慢慢暗了下去，如同在一面水上走路。他走得很轻很轻，也不知为什么，总觉得这里的东西都在睡觉，不该吵醒了它们。

便在这时，他看见了光。山谷最深处，一片给雨水砸出来的浅坑里，有一点银光一明一暗，一明一暗，像有什么东西在很慢很慢地呼吸。
story_full.en:
Xiaoman didn't even think — no, that's wrong. He thought, and he thought fast, as fast as his mother working the beads of an abacus: Pa two steps away, the drop past the slope. Pull him, and maybe they'd both go over. Don't pull him, and he'd certainly go over. It wasn't a hard sum.

Quicker than it takes to tell, Xiaoman threw himself forward, grabbed his father's belt and hauled inward with everything he had, hauled so hard that his father slammed into the cliff face with an "Oof!" — and the force of it swung Xiaoman himself out and away. His father spun round and grabbed for him. His fingers brushed Xiaoman's wrist, and in the end they didn't catch it.

Xiaoman fell. Mud, stones, broken branches and rain came at him from every side; sky and earth turned more somersaults in front of his eyes than he could count, until he couldn't tell which way was up. He covered his head. His back slammed into something hard, so painful everything went black. He grabbed blindly and actually caught hold of a vine.

The vine went taut and, for one moment, it jerked his fall to a stop; then it snapped.{景=zhuigu}

At the last he landed in something soft. It was moss, a layer of it, very thick and very soft, like a huge quilt that had soaked up all the water it could hold. He sank half a foot into it, like an ant fallen into a giant steamed bun.

He didn't get up straight away. His father had said: when you fall, don't rush to get up; check yourself, one thing at a time. First he moved his fingers; the fingers moved. Then his toes; the toes moved too. His knees were skinned, a layer of skin was scraped off his palms, his back was burning, and his left wrist had swollen up high — broken or not, he couldn't feel, but at least it still moved.

Only then did he sit up and look up. The cliff was too high to see the top; it vanished into the rain and mist.

He didn't shout. He just did the sum in his head: Pa had been hauled into the cliff face by him and hadn't fallen. With his bad knee and rain this heavy, he couldn't get down, and shouldn't try. He'd wait for the rain to stop, follow the marks back to the village, and fetch help. Forty-one marks, cut by his own hand, not one of them crooked — except the first. So what he had to do was stay alive until then.

Twelve years old, alone, in a valley he'd never been to, and night coming on. His father had said that when a hunter gets lost in the mountains, the first thing is to find somewhere out of the rain, the second is to make a fire, and only the third is to be afraid. Xiaoman decided the third thing could stay owing for now.

The rain eased a little. He felt about on the ground for a sharp stone and went on along the foot of the cliff, one hand on the rock, and every so often he scratched a line on the cliff face so he'd remember the way back.

He'd gone less than half a li when, in the moss at the foot of the cliff, the sharp stone struck something hard with a *clink*. He scraped the moss away. It was a fire steel, rusted red; its sheath had long since rotted away, and beside it was a flint wrapped in oilcloth, the oilcloth half rotted too.

On the wooden handle of the fire steel a character had been cut with a knife, crooked and wobbly, and he knew it. It was the first character his mother had taught him to write: **Shen**. He crouched there looking at it for a long time. In Shi'ao Village there was only one household named Shen, and of the Shens only one had gone into Black Pine Ridge and not come back.

He remembered Granny Wu saying "The year your grandpa went, he passed my door too", and his palms went cold. Grandpa had been here. Grandpa had died in this valley. He tucked the fire steel and the flint inside his jacket. He didn't tell anyone about it, ever.

This valley was very strange. The mountains outside grew pine and cypress and wild chestnut, but here he didn't know a single tree. Their leaves were silver-white, so thin the light came through them, and rain that landed on them didn't run off but rolled into round beads that hung from the tips.

He couldn't help himself; he reached out and touched one. There was a faint *ting*, like a very, very tiny bell, and the bead turned into a wisp of white vapour and was gone without a trace.

The grass on the ground was different too. With every step, the blades gave off a faint light, and a pale ring of it spread out from under his foot and slowly faded again, as if he were walking on water. He walked very, very lightly. He didn't know why, but he felt that everything here was asleep, and he shouldn't wake it.

And then he saw the light. In the deepest part of the valley, in a shallow hollow the rain had battered out of the ground, a point of silver light was glowing and dimming, glowing and dimming, as if something were breathing very, very slowly.
